explanations.explanation: Job 38:1 says the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind. After all those chapters of waiting for a reply, it arrives in the middle of a storm wind. Nobody in that moment is checking their phone. I think Job stops talking and listens.

That's how the LORD got Moses' attention, Israel's leader, from flames inside a bush (Exodus 3:2-4). Easy to mix up, since both are the LORD speaking out of something dramatic. For Job, though, the text says the LORD answered him out of the whirlwind (Job 38:1). Different stage, same LORD.

explanations.answer: Out of a pillar of cloud
explanations.explanation: A pillar of cloud is what went before Israel by day in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21). It's a good guess, since a cloud and a wind are cousins. But Job 38:1 says the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind. A pillar stands still, and a whirlwind does NOT.

Careful, friend. To obscure something is to make it cloudy, so the LORD is saying the opposite of clearer. He asks who obscures His counsel by words without knowledge (Job 38:2). That's like wiping a window with a muddy rag and calling it clean.

That's right. The text says Job's words obscure the LORD's counsel, which means they make it harder to see (Job 38:2). Words without knowledge don't clear anything up. It's like pointing at a map with a very confident finger and a very wrong idea of where you are.

It goes the other way around. Job wanted to be the one asking, and he asked for a hearing with God (Job 13:3). But the LORD says, “I will question you, and you shall inform Me.” So Job isn't getting an answer sheet. He's getting the questions.

Right on the money, baker. The LORD says, “I will question you, and you shall inform Me.” The roles flip. Job came ready to ask, and now the LORD is the one asking, and Job is the one who has to answer.

Measurements, a measuring line, foundations and a cornerstone are all words from putting up a building. The LORD asks who fixed the earth's measurements and who stretched a measuring line across it (Job 38:5). Then He asks who laid its cornerstone. Picture a construction site with the whole earth on it.

No river anywhere in these verses. A river flows, and a flowing thing doesn't get a cornerstone. The LORD is using measuring line and cornerstone words, which belong to a building (Job 38:5-6). The sea does show up soon, but that's a different question.

A flock would need a shepherd, and these verses don't have one. The LORD talks about measurements, a measuring line, foundations and a cornerstone (Job 38:5-6). Nobody lays a cornerstone for a flock. If you did, that would be one very confused sheep.

Job 38:7 says the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy. That's a celebration, and everybody is in on it. Job wasn't there for it, and that's the LORD's point. The stars sing, the sons of God shout, and the cornerstone goes down.

There's no fear in this scene. The morning stars sing together, and all the sons of God shout for joy (Job 38:7). Weeping is a fine thing in other places, but this verse is a party. When a cornerstone goes down, the crowd cheers.

Nothing in this verse is quiet. The morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy (Job 38:7). Silence would be a very different scene. This one is LOUD, and it's loud with gladness.

The LORD says He fixed the sea's boundaries and set in place its bars and doors (Job 38:10). The sea bursts out, and it gets a limit. Bars and doors are things you put on a space to keep something where it belongs. It's like handing a very big, very loud guest a very clear address.
The text goes the opposite way. The LORD fixes the sea's boundaries and sets in place its bars and doors (Job 38:10). A sea with bars and doors isn't covering everything. It has a place to stay.
The sea doesn't disappear here. The LORD fixes its boundaries and sets in place its bars and doors (Job 38:10). The sea stays, and it stays inside a limit. Drying it up wouldn't need any bars at all.

Yes, the LORD speaks right to the sea. He declares, “You may come this far, but no farther…” (Job 38:11). Then He tells the proud waves they must stop. Most of us can't get a toddler to stop at the end of a hallway, and here's the whole sea with a limit.

It's true, friend. In Job 38:11 the LORD declares, “You may come this far, but no farther…” and He says it to the sea. The proud waves are told where they must stop. The sea gets a clear line and the LORD is the One who draws it.

explanations.answer: To the vents of the sea
explanations.explanation: The LORD asks, “Have you journeyed to the vents of the sea…” (Job 38:16). It's a trip down to the deep places of the ocean. Job hasn't made it, and neither has anybody I know. I once thought the back of a drawer was far down.

explanations.answer: To the bottom of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: The Jordan is a river, and it's not named in these verses. The LORD asks about the vents of the sea and the trenches of the deep (Job 38:16). He's talking about the ocean floor. The deep here is far bigger than any one river.

Machpelah is a cave where Abraham buried his wife Sarah (Genesis 23:19). It's a real place, but it's not where the LORD sends Job's thoughts. He asks about the vents of the sea and the trenches of the deep (Job 38:16). That's a much bigger hole.

That's what He asks. “Have the gates of death been revealed to you?” (Job 38:17). The next question says it again with the shadow of death. This is a heavy place to go, so I'll just say it plainly: the LORD is asking about something Job hasn't seen.

It is in there. The LORD asks, “Have the gates of death been revealed to you?” (Job 38:17). Then He asks whether Job has seen the gates of the shadow of death. It's a weighty question, and the text says it twice.

The LORD asks, “Where is the way to the home of light?” (Job 38:19). Then He asks about the paths to darkness's home (Job 38:20). Light and darkness are each pictured with a place to go home to. I think that's a pretty picture, like both of them have a porch.

No throne in these verses. The LORD talks about the home of light and the paths to darkness's home (Job 38:19-20). A throne would be about ruling, and a home is about where something lives. Light and darkness get a home each.

A field would need a farmer, and nobody's planting here. The LORD asks about the home of light and the paths to the home of darkness (Job 38:19-20). Light and darkness each have a home, with paths leading to it. No crops required.

That's it. The LORD already asked, “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4). Now He says, “Surely you know, for you were already born!” I think it's a pointed line. Job wasn't there for the foundations.

explanations.answer: Job is older than the earth
explanations.explanation: That would flip the whole thing around. The LORD asked Job where he was when He laid the foundations of the earth (Job 38:4). The point is that Job wasn't there. Nobody comes out of that question older than the dirt.

explanations.answer: Job learned it from his elders
explanations.explanation: There's nobody's elders in these verses. The LORD is pointing back to His question about where Job was when the foundations of the earth were laid (Job 38:4). He says, “Surely you know, for you were already born!” The point is Job's own timing, not his teachers.

Not quite. The LORD says He holds the snow and hail in reserve for times of trouble, for the day of war and battle (Job 38:22-23). Reserve means saved up for a purpose. So it's not just wherever they please, friend.

Right. The LORD says He holds the snow and hail in reserve, and He names times of trouble and the day of war and battle (Job 38:23). Reserve means set aside and kept. It's like a stack of cookie boxes waiting by the door for the big day.
It's the other way around. The LORD brings rain on a barren land and on a desert where no man lives (Job 38:26). That's rain where nobody's home to use it. People aren't the only reason He sends it.

Yes, friend. The LORD says He brings rain on a barren land, on a desert where no man lives (Job 38:26). Then He says it makes the parched wasteland sprout with tender grass (Job 38:27). The rain falls where nobody's around to see it.

That's the picture. “Does the rain have a father? Who has begotten the drops of dew?” (Job 38:28). Then He asks from whose womb the ice emerges and who gives birth to the frost (Job 38:29). Father, womb and birth. The weather gets a baby album.

Fire isn't in these verses at all. The LORD talks about a father, begetting, a womb and giving birth (Job 38:28-29). That's the language of being born. Ice coming out of a forge would be a very confusing day.

Planting would use seeds and dirt, and neither shows up in these questions. The LORD asks about a father, a womb and giving birth (Job 38:28-29). That's the picture of being born. Frost doesn't get planted, it gets born.
The text says the opposite. The LORD speaks of the waters becoming hard as stone and the surface of the deep being frozen (Job 38:30). So it does freeze. Water as hard as stone is a lot to picture.

That's right. The LORD says the waters become hard as stone and the surface of the deep is frozen (Job 38:30). Water that hard sounds like something you'd stub a toe on. And He asks who gives birth to the frost from heaven (Job 38:29).

That's the question. “Do you know the laws of the heavens?” (Job 38:33). Then He asks if Job can set their dominion over the earth. Laws for the sky is a big idea. I can barely get a cookie timer to behave.

explanations.answer: The names of all the angels
explanations.explanation: Angels don't show up in this question. The LORD asks, “Do you know the laws of the heavens?” (Job 38:33). He's still looking at the sky and its order. Names aren't what He's asking about.

Sand doesn't come up here. The LORD asks Job if he knows the laws of the heavens and if he can set their dominion over the earth (Job 38:33). Counting is a different question from knowing laws. Stay up in the sky with Him on this one.

He does ask it. “Can you send the lightning bolts on their way? Do they report to you, ‘Here we are’?” (Job 38:35). Picture lightning checking in like an employee on Monday morning. Job can't call it, and that's the point of the question.

It's in the text, friend. The LORD asks, “Can you send the lightning bolts on their way? Do they report to you, ‘Here we are’?” (Job 38:35). Lightning isn't taking orders from Job. The question is about who they do answer to.

explanations.answer: Who put wisdom in the heart
explanations.explanation: That's the question that stands out. “Who has put wisdom in the heart or given understanding to the mind?” (Job 38:36). It comes right in the middle of the clouds and lightning. All that knowing Job was asking about had to come from somewhere.

That happened too, but not here. Adam, the first man, gave names to the livestock, the birds and the beasts (Genesis 2:20). In Job 38:36 the LORD asks who has put wisdom in the heart or given understanding to the mind. Different question, same LORD.

The Bible does tell us about that. Cain, Adam's son, became the builder of a city (Genesis 4:17). But in Job 38:36 the LORD asks who has put wisdom in the heart or given understanding to the mind. No bricks in that question.

Yes. The LORD asks who can tilt the water jars of the heavens (Job 38:37). Tilt a jar of water over dust and you get rain on hard ground. The dust hardens into a mass, and the clods stick together (Job 38:38). I think it's a very good picture of a dry yard and a downpour.
Light was back in the earlier questions, with its own home (Job 38:19). This one is about water jars of the heavens being tilted (Job 38:37). Light doesn't pour out of a jar. Water does.

No fire here, friend. The LORD asks who can tilt the water jars of the heavens (Job 38:37). Water jars hold water, and tilting them is how you get rain. Fire on hardened dust would be a whole different story.
